doc.title: John LaPorta interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

chapter: Race, feel and playing with Mingus
title: Black and white band feel, Dixieland and Mingus's church remark
summary: He contrasts feeling music in four versus two, from New Orleans onward, and tells of the one argument with Charles Mingus about a drummer who went to the wrong church.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Was there a noticeable difference at the time between let’s say the bands like Glenn Miller and the white oriented bands and Basie and Ellington that you can talk about?

Well there certainly was. A good example would be Dixieland music. I never realized until I made a study, I wanted to do a New Orleans concert at the school after being there for twenty-five years and never having seen one at Berklee, I guess it was a modern school for that time, I decided to do a New Orleans concert. And the students really loved it because it was so different from what they heard there. But in the process of preparing for it, I got to realize that the thing about feeling music in four-four rather than in two- four, and you know what I mean by that, was not something, a product of our time, but existed from the very beginning. You go back to Jelly Roll Morton and the New Orleans music, a lot of it feels, the black music feels in four-four. The white influences are in two. Mingus one time, the only time I ever — Charles Mingus — the only time I ever had an argument with him was when he was not happy about a drummer he used because I had used him on a record date and then he didn’t like him on the thing. And finally he screamed at me he says, “Don’t you realize he goes to the wrong church?” So you know if you go into middle America and you listen to country music or whatever, you’ll find that the concentration of accents, rhythmically, are on one and three. And if you go into a black church, the concentration of accents are on two and four. And this is what he was referring to. I broke up and that was the end of the argument see.
